table.text: As part of the PEACH study, participants were randomly assigned to the PEACH intervention group (n = 655) or a waitlist control group (n = 218).

Participants were eligible if they (a) were at least 18 years old, (b) could read German, (c) were not receiving psychotherapeutic or psychiatric treatment, (d) owned a smartphone (Android or iOS) with mobile internet access, and (e) were interested and motivated to participate in an intervention to change a personality trait.
Participants were recruited through university mailings, social media advertisements, flyers, and word-of-mouth.

To assess demographic characteristics, participants were asked about their age, gender (coded as0 = male,1 = female), education level (coded as0 = not university,1 = university), and relationship status (coded as0 = not in a relationship,1 = in a relationship).
Participants were asked to forward a weblink to the questionnaire to friends, family members, or their intimate partner, with no limit on the number of recipients.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.title: Non-Significant P Value Check
stat_p_nonsig.summary_text: We found 9 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

table.expanded: The average treatment effect on life satisfaction was positive but not significant (Estimate = 0.133, SE = 0.106, d = 0.121, p = .212), and there was no evidence for heterogeneity of individual treatment effects, Wald χ²(1) = 0.21, p = .648.

The average treatment effect on life satisfaction was positive but not significant (Estimate = 0.133, SE = 0.106, d = 0.121, p = .212), and there was no evidence for heterogeneity of individual treatment effects, Wald χ²(1) = 0.21, p = .648.

On the outlier-and carelessness-corrected data, the cross-validated optimum dropped to k = 0, yielding a baseline-only model with a significant average effect (Estimate = 0.151, SE = 0.074, p = .042) but no significant heterogeneity, Wald χ²(1) = 0.89, p = .347.
The association with self-reported Intellectual Curiosity was of similar size as observer-reported Openness but not significant (r = .49, p = .058).
First, for gender, the average treatment effect was significant for men (0.249, p = .007) but not for women (0.080, p = .311; difference: -0.17, p = .027).

Third, for change goal attainability, the negative association arose because higher attainability predicted greater expected improvement under the control condition (r = .25, p = .005) but was unrelated to expected change under the intervention (r = -.06, p = .551).

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 310 columns across 14 data files.
#### Careless Responding

128 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **106 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

**What this does not cover.** Only 1 of 14 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 3 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  0 of 2 scripts ran without error when executed (1 more is run by another script with `source()`).
-  14 installable dependencies detected.

live_data_statements: In (b), orange (medium gray) diamonds indicate estimates of improvements, if participants were in the control group, and yellow (light gray) diamonds, if participants were in the intervention group.
As part of the PEACH study, participants were randomly assigned to the PEACH intervention group (n = 655) or a waitlist control group (n = 218).

Participants were eligible if they (a) were at least 18 years old, (b) could read German, (c) were not receiving psychotherapeutic or psychiatric treatment, (d) owned a smartphone (Android or iOS) with mobile internet access, and (e) were interested and motivated to participate in an intervention to change a personality trait.
Participants were recruited through university mailings, social media advertisements, flyers, and word-of-mouth.

To assess demographic characteristics, participants were asked about their age, gender (coded as0 = male,1 = female), education level (coded as0 = not university,1 = university), and relationship status (coded as0 = not in a relationship,1 = in a relationship).
Participants were asked to forward a weblink to the questionnaire to friends, family members, or their intimate partner, with no limit on the number of recipients.
In addition, participants were asked to rate their satisfaction with nine specific life domains, each assessed with a single item ( Hudson & Roberts, 2014
Eligible participants completed a pretest assessment and selected a personality change goal, supported by descriptions of typical characteristics associated with high and low trait levels.
In the waitlist control group, participants completed the pretest, waited four weeks, and then filled out the posttestfoot_0.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 3 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:3, File = c("covariate_selection_cv_v2.R", 
"peach r script final 2.r", "run_analysis.R"), "Runs after" = c("—", 
"—", "covariate_selection_cv_v2.R"), Basis = c("numeric", "numeric", 
"dependency")), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**2 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `data_paper.csv` to `../Data/data_paper.csv` (in peach r script final 2.r); `covariate_selection_cv_v2.r` to `covariate_selection_cv_v2.R` (in run_analysis.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. **4 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.

**1 file name in the code is not the same as in the deposit**, in case, spaces or punctuation, and exactly one file in the deposit fits. To run the code we corrected this in a copy of the script so that it finds the file. The script itself should be changed, because as written it does not find the file on every system.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "run_analysis.R", "Name in the code" = "covariate_selection_cv_v2.r", 
    "Name in the deposit" = "covariate_selection_cv_v2.R"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### Files the deposit does not hold
The scripts that did not run through read 2 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `data.rds`, `data_cleaned.rds`.
#### Files not run on their own
1 file only defines functions, so running it on its own says nothing: a function counts when a script uses it. These files are not counted as scripts. 0 are used by no script in the deposit.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "covariate_selection_cv_v2.R", "Used by" = "peach r script final 2.r, run_analysis.R"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 3 scripts: 0 ran without error, 2 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 1 was run by another script with `source()`. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("covariate_selection_cv_v2.R", "peach r script final 2.r", 
"run_analysis.R"), Outcome = c("run_by_source", "errored", "errored"
), Detail = c("", "runtime", "runtime"), "Time (s)" = c(0, 85.7, 
3.6)), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**1 script calls `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "peach r script final 2.r", "setwd() removed" = 1L, 
    "Path(s) it set" = "PROJECT DIRECTORY"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**Run by another script**

1 script is run by another script with `source()`, so it was not run on its own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on its own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Its outcome is part of the sourcing script's outcome.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "covariate_selection_cv_v2.R", "Run by" = "run_analysis.R"), row.names = "covariate_selection_cv_v2.R", class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```

>   
>   mm <- generateMeasurementModel(indicators=zl, ncells=2)  # specify joint latent covariates model (with free residual variances across groups)
>   tmp <- paste0(paste0(names(zl), collapse=" + "), " ~ c(NA,NA)*1") ## add lv means
>   fm <- paste0(ym, "\n", mm, "\n", tmp)  # specify full model (i.e. joint model of outcomes and covariates)

>   max.k <- (length(zo)+length(zl)+1)*2+1  # maximum number of predictors in the model

>   rsq.traindat <- vector("list",nrep)

>   
>   # predict-function for regsubsets-object (from package leaps)
>   predict.regsubsets <- function(object, newdata, id, ...){
>     mat <- model.matrix(change~., newdata)
>     coefi <- coef(object, id=id)
>     xvars <- names(coefi)
>     mat[,xvars] %*% coefi
>   }
>   
>   
>   # repetitions
>   
>   for (r in 1:nrep) {
>     
>     rsq.traindat[[r]] <- data.frame(matrix(NA,max.k,nfold))
>     mse.traindat[[r]] <- data.frame(matrix(NA,max.k,nfold))

>     
>     folds <- sample(1:nfold, nrow(dat), replace =TRUE)
>     
>     # folds
>

>         # extract factor scores from separate models in training data
>         
>         trainfs <- lavPredict(fit.ym, method="Regression", assemble=TRUE)

>         trainfs.mm[,group] <- NULL

>         
>       } else {
>         
>         if (fs.method == "js") {
>           
>           # estimates joint model and extract separate fs in training data

>           trainfs <- lavPredict(fit.fm, method="Regression", assemble=TRUE, separate=TRUE)  # use only info from relevant parcels
>           
>         } else {
>           
>           if (fs.method == "j") {
>             
>             # estimates joint model and extract standard fs in training data

>             fit.fm <- lavaan::sem(model = fm, traindat, missing = "fiml", estimator = "MLR",group = group, group.label = c("0","1"), meanstructure = TRUE)

>           }
>           
>         }
>       }
>       
>       # compute adjusted change scores in training data
>       
>       trainfs[,group] <- as.numeric(trainfs[,group])
>       trainfs$change <- trainfs[,"y.pos"] - trainfs[,"y.pre"]

text.text: Part of the data has been published as part of previous publications (for a full list, see the supplemental materials).

In a study among 873 adults, participating in a digital personality change program improved satisfaction across different areas of life for about 27% of participants, whereas it had no effects for 66%, and negative effects for 7%.
Benefits were largest for men, participants rated as more open by others, and those who felt their goal was harder to reach on their own.
Personality traits have a profound influence on a person's experience and behavior.
As a result, there is growing interest in interventions to change these traits into an individually desirable direction.

With a growing number of studies on volitional personality change (e.g., Haehner et al., 2025; Hudson et al., 2019; Stieger et al., 2021), researchers have recently begun investigating whether personality change interventions have secondary effects on other important outcomes, such as well-being (Olaru, van Scheppingen, Stieger, et al., 2023).
text.formatted: With a growing number of studies on volitional personality change (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Haehner et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Hudson et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Stieger et al., 2021)</ref>, researchers have recently begun investigating whether personality change interventions have secondary effects on other important outcomes, such as well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Olaru, van Scheppingen, Stieger, et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, this research has focused on average effects, such as whether personality change interventions lead to increases in life satisfaction for an average person (Olaru, van Scheppingen, Stieger, et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Notably, this research has focused on average effects, such as whether personality change interventions lead to increases in life satisfaction for an average person <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Olaru, van Scheppingen, Stieger, et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, little is known about the extent to which these effects differ between individuals and which baseline characteristics predict these differences.

Given the heterogeneity of treatment effects observed in related research areas (e.g., psychotherapy research; Kaiser et al., 2022), a systematic investigation of interindividual differences in the effectiveness of personality change interventions seems promising.
text.formatted: Given the heterogeneity of treatment effects observed in related research areas (e.g., psychotherapy research; <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Kaiser et al., 2022)</ref>, a systematic investigation of interindividual differences in the effectiveness of personality change interventions seems promising.

text.text: Such research is crucial for tailored dissemination and further personalization of interventions according to the individual characteristics of potential users (Matz et al., 2024; Modersitzki et al., 2025).

text.text: First evidence for the changeability of personality traits via interventions comes from clinical psychology.
For instance, a systematic review of 207 studies found decreases in Neuroticism and increases in Extraversion as a result of interventions targeting mental health problems (Roberts et al., 2017).
text.formatted: For instance, a systematic review of 207 studies found decreases in Neuroticism and increases in Extraversion as a result of interventions targeting mental health problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Roberts et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: More recent research has shifted from examining personality change as a secondary outcome of clinical treatments to focusing on targeted personality change through dedicated interventions.

These studies showed that personality traits can be altered in non-clinical populations (for a review see Haehner et al., 2024), for instance, by regularly setting specific goals (i.e., implementation intentions) for personality change (Hudson & Fraley, 2015) or completing behavioral activation tasks (Hudson et al., 2019).
text.formatted: These studies showed that personality traits can be altered in non-clinical populations (for a review see <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Haehner et al., 2024)</ref>, for instance, by regularly setting specific goals (i.e., implementation intentions) for personality change <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hudson & Fraley, 2015)</ref> or completing behavioral activation tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Hudson et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with these ideas, a 10-week personality change intervention using the smartphone application PErsonality coACH (PEACH; Stieger et al., 2018 Stieger et al., , 2021) ) led to personality change in the individually desired direction, especially by decreasing Neuroticism and increasing Extraversion and Conscientiousness (Stieger et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Consistent with these ideas, a 10-week personality change intervention using the smartphone application PErsonality coACH (PEACH; <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Stieger et al., 2018</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Stieger et al., , 2021) )</ref> led to personality change in the individually desired direction, especially by decreasing Neuroticism and increasing Extraversion and Conscientiousness <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Stieger et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, the changes remained stable at 3-month and 1-year follow-up assessments (Stieger et al., 2021 (Stieger et al., , 2024) ) and were partly also observed by close others (Stieger et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Moreover, the changes remained stable at 3-month and 1-year follow-up assessments <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Stieger et al., 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Stieger et al., , 2024) )</ref> and were partly also observed by close others <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Stieger et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These results support the idea that personality traits can be modified via interventions.
Beyond changes in personality traits, a central goal of personality change interventions is to produce effects on consequential life outcomes (Bleidorn et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Beyond changes in personality traits, a central goal of personality change interventions is to produce effects on consequential life outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bleidorn et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Life satisfaction (i.e., a person's subjective evaluation of their own life overall) has emerged as a particularly important outcome (Olaru, van Scheppingen, Stieger, et al., 2023) for at least three reasons: First, life satisfaction is a central component of subjective well-being (Diener et al., 1999 (Diener et al., , 2018)), which is frequently studied in both personality and intervention research (Anglim et al., 2020; Carr et al., 2024) and linked to other consequential life outcomes such as physical health, longevity, and job performance (Diener et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Life satisfaction (i.e., a person's subjective evaluation of their own life overall) has emerged as a particularly important outcome <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Olaru, van Scheppingen, Stieger, et al., 2023)</ref> for at least three reasons: First, life satisfaction is a central component of subjective well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Diener et al., 1999</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Diener et al., , 2018))</ref>, which is frequently studied in both personality and intervention research <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Anglim et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Carr et al., 2024)</ref> and linked to other consequential life outcomes such as physical health, longevity, and job performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Diener et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Second, previous research has shown that interindividual differences in personality traits are robustly associated with differences in life satisfaction in both cross-sectional and longitudinal observational studies (Anglim et al., 2020; Olaru, van Scheppingen, Bleidorn, et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Second, previous research has shown that interindividual differences in personality traits are robustly associated with differences in life satisfaction in both cross-sectional and longitudinal observational studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Anglim et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Olaru, van Scheppingen, Bleidorn, et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, the causality and directionality of this effect (i.e., personality affecting life satisfaction or vice versa) remain unclear (Soto, 2015).
text.formatted: However, the causality and directionality of this effect (i.e., personality affecting life satisfaction or vice versa) remain unclear <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Soto, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Experimental interventions that manipulate personality traits and assess effects on life satisfaction offer one of the few empirical strategies for testing the personality-to-life-satisfaction pathway, thereby informing causal theories about the relationship between personality and well-being.

Third, individuals with stronger change goals tend to report lower life satisfaction (Hudson & Roberts, 2014), suggesting that individuals may pursue personality change interventions as a way to enhance their well-being.
text.formatted: Third, individuals with stronger change goals tend to report lower life satisfaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Hudson & Roberts, 2014)</ref>, suggesting that individuals may pursue personality change interventions as a way to enhance their well-being.

text.text: This perspective aligns with self-regulatory models of personality development, which propose that individuals can be motivated to change if they view new behaviors as instrumental in achieving other goals such as increasing their well-being (Hennecke et al., 2014).
text.formatted: This perspective aligns with self-regulatory models of personality development, which propose that individuals can be motivated to change if they view new behaviors as instrumental in achieving other goals such as increasing their well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Hennecke et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: If improving life satisfaction is a key motivator for participation, then life satisfaction is also a meaningful criterion by which participants themselves would judge intervention success.

In addition to global satisfaction with life as a whole, satisfaction can be assessed with respect to specific life domains (e.g., school/work, health, recreational activities, friendships; Hudson & Roberts, 2014).
text.formatted: In addition to global satisfaction with life as a whole, satisfaction can be assessed with respect to specific life domains (e.g., school/work, health, recreational activities, friendships; <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Hudson & Roberts, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Because some of these domains are directly targeted by the intervention, domain-specific satisfaction may be more proximal to the intervention and therefore more sensitive to change than global life satisfaction.

Consistent with bottom-up theories of well-being (Diener, 1984; Diener et al., 1999; Schimmack, 2008), these domainspecific satisfactions can be combined into a composite measure of average life domain satisfaction.
text.formatted: Consistent with bottom-up theories of well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Diener, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Diener et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Schimmack, 2008)</ref>, these domainspecific satisfactions can be combined into a composite measure of average life domain satisfaction.

text.text: Recently, researchers have begun to study the effects of personality change interventions on well-being, though there are still few studies that directly test this hypothesis.

Notably, a study examining the effects of the PEACH intervention on life and domain satisfaction in the three largest intervention groups found that satisfaction increased from pretest to follow-up but remained stable in the control group, and that changes in satisfaction were positively correlated with changes in personality traits (Olaru, van Scheppingen, Stieger, et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Notably, a study examining the effects of the PEACH intervention on life and domain satisfaction in the three largest intervention groups found that satisfaction increased from pretest to follow-up but remained stable in the control group, and that changes in satisfaction were positively correlated with changes in personality traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Olaru, van Scheppingen, Stieger, et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The studies described above have focused on average treatment effects, that is, the expected effect of the intervention for an average person.
However, little is known about (a) the extent to which personality intervention effects differ between individuals, and (b) which characteristics are associated with these differences.

Work in related areas, such as psychotherapy research, shows considerable heterogeneity in intervention effects across individuals (Cohen & DeRubeis, 2018; Kaiser et al., 2022; Mayer et al., 2020), with some showing pronounced benefits and others displaying minimal or even adverse responses.
text.formatted: Work in related areas, such as psychotherapy research, shows considerable heterogeneity in intervention effects across individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cohen & DeRubeis, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Kaiser et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Mayer et al., 2020)</ref>, with some showing pronounced benefits and others displaying minimal or even adverse responses.

text.text: A better knowledge of these interindividual differences is essential for personalizing interventions (Matz et al., 2024; Modersitzki et al., 2025).
text.formatted: A better knowledge of these interindividual differences is essential for personalizing interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Matz et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Modersitzki et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, examining interindividual differences is crucial to ensure that interventions (a) benefit diverse populations without systematically disadvantaging any groups-including marginalized or disadvantaged ones-and (b) do not produce unintended harmful effects (e.g., decreases in well-being for certain individuals), which have not been examined systematically for personality change interventions (Haehner et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In addition, examining interindividual differences is crucial to ensure that interventions (a) benefit diverse populations without systematically disadvantaging any groups-including marginalized or disadvantaged ones-and (b) do not produce unintended harmful effects (e.g., decreases in well-being for certain individuals), which have not been examined systematically for personality change interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Haehner et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: When studying the role of interindividual differences for intervention outcomes, two different strategies can be employed: the prognostic approach and the prescriptive approach (Fournier et al., 2009; Kraemer et al., 2002;  see Figure 1 for a graphical illustration).
text.formatted: When studying the role of interindividual differences for intervention outcomes, two different strategies can be employed: the prognostic approach and the prescriptive approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Fournier et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Kraemer et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> for a graphical illustration).

text.text: First, the prognostic approach examines which interindividual differences at baseline (e.g., sociodemographic variables, baseline personality traits) predict the outcome (e.g., improvement in satisfaction) among individuals receiving the intervention (e.g., Olaru et al., 2025).
text.formatted: First, the prognostic approach examines which interindividual differences at baseline (e.g., sociodemographic variables, baseline personality traits) predict the outcome (e.g., improvement in satisfaction) among individuals receiving the intervention (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Olaru et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In other words, it addresses the question: Based on a set of interindividual difference characteristics, how much is this person likely to improve over the course of the intervention?
Importantly, this approach does not take into account what outcome a participant would show if they were assigned to a comparison condition, such as an alternative treatment or a waitlist control.
Baseline characteristics that predict improvement under the intervention may therefore reflect general predictors of improvement rather than a specific benefit from the intervention.
Second, the prescriptive approach focuses on examining which interindividual differences at baseline predict the treatment effect relative to a control condition.
More specifically, this approach asks: Which interindividual difference characteristics predict the extent to which the intervention yields more favorable outcomes than the control condition?

In personality change interventions, this would involve comparing participants' expected satisfaction levels in the intervention group with their expected satisfaction levels in the control group (e.g., waitlist or active comparison treatment) and then investigating which interindividual differences at baseline predict this difference (see example studies Mayer et al., 2020; Zainal et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In personality change interventions, this would involve comparing participants' expected satisfaction levels in the intervention group with their expected satisfaction levels in the control group (e.g., waitlist or active comparison treatment) and then investigating which interindividual differences at baseline predict this difference (see example studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Mayer et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Zainal et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Statistically, this corresponds to a moderation effect, that is, whether interindividual difference variables moderate the effect of intervention vs. control condition on the outcome.

While the prognostic approach allows prognoses about the expected improvement of enrolled individuals, the prescriptive approach allows predictions about the optimal treatment choice (e.g., enrollment in intervention vs. control group) for different individuals to begin with, which makes it particularly informative for personalizing intervention choice.
Therefore, this paper focuses solely on prescriptive variables.

Given the scarcity of well-established theories and empirical findings regarding moderators of personality change interventions, we employ an exploratory approach to investigate a wide range of interindividual differences that may predict intervention effects.

In (a), filled yellow (light gray) circles represent observations from the intervention group; the dashed line shows the fitted trend as a function of baseline Conscientiousness scores.
In (b), orange (medium gray) diamonds indicate estimates of improvements, if participants were in the control group, and yellow (light gray) diamonds, if participants were in the intervention group.
Blue (dark gray) vertical lines link each participant's paired estimated outcomes for the control and intervention group.

Blue (dark gray) diamonds represent estimates of the individual treatment effect, i.e., differential improvements in life satisfaction depending on whether participants would be part of the intervention or control group.
Two illustrative cases are highlighted.
Person A starts the PEACH intervention with high levels of Conscientiousness at baseline, whereas person B starts with low levels of Conscientiousness.
After the PEACH intervention, A scores high in life satisfaction and shows greater improvements than B, likely because A engaged conscientiously with the intervention.

If assigned to the control group, A would still score high in life satisfaction at post-measurement, as A's high Conscientiousness would lead them to find alternative ways to pursue their intervention goals.
Consequently, A's expected treatment effect (i.e., the difference between estimated intervention and control group outcomes) is relatively small.
Similarly, person B shows improvements in life satisfaction after the PEACH intervention, suggesting that B likely met their goal through the intervention.
However, if assigned to the control group, B would score low in life satisfaction at post-measurement, as their lower Conscientiousness makes alternative self-directed change less likely.
Thus, B's expected individual treatment effect is larger than A's.

Second, baseline levels of personality traits may influence how participants engage with the intervention.
For instance, conscientious individuals are more organized and dutiful, which can support adherence and consistent practice (Högdahl et al., 2016).

text.text: To the extent that greater engagement leads to stronger change during the intervention (Hudson et al., 2019; Olaru et al., 2025), baseline personality may be prognostic of individuals' improvement.

text.text: Third, prior clinical work has shown that baseline well-being can affect treatment effects.

For instance, in meta-analyses, participants with greater symptom severity (i.e., lower well-being) before the start of the study benefited more from interventions relative to control conditions (e.g., Scholten et al., 2023).

text.text: Fourth, self-regulatory models of personality development suggest that participants' motivation for change as well as the considered feasibility of these changes should affect how much participants change their personality during an intervention (Hennecke et al., 2014).

text.text: Lastly, as self-reflective processes and behavioral activities represent key intervention pathways that enhance understanding of personal challenges and facilitate active problem solving (e.g., Allemand & Flückiger, 2017), participants' preferences for self-reflective versus behavioral engagement may shape how they respond to the intervention.

text.text: For personality traits, motivational factors, and engagement preferences, these arguments thus primarily suggest prognostic associations.
Whether these characteristics are also prescriptive, that is, predict treatment effects, depends on whether they facilitate change without the intervention as well (see Figure 1).

text.text: In the present study, we examine the degree to which the effects of personality change interventions on life and domain satisfaction differ between individuals.

We use longitudinal data from the 10-week personality change intervention PEACH (Stieger et al., 2018 (Stieger et al., , 2021) ) to estimate average and individual treatment effects of the intervention (vs. waitlist control) on life satisfaction, average domain satisfaction, and satisfaction with individual domains using the EffectLiteR approach, a multi-group structural equation modeling framework for causal inference (Mayer et al., 2016 (Mayer et al., , 2020)).

text.text: We test, quantify, and visualize the degree of interindividual differences in treatment effects and, crucially, predict treatment effects from baseline variables assessed at pretest, consistent with a prescriptive approach.

For baseline variables, we focus on demographic characteristics (age, gender, relationship status, education level), baseline personality traits (Big Five self-and observer-reports), baseline well-being (satisfaction, self-esteem), motivational factors (change goal strength, change goal commitment and attainability, belief about the changeability of personality), and engagement preferences (preference for self-reflective and behavioral engagement).

text.text: Two individuals did not complete the baseline questionnaires or completed them only partially, resulting in a final sample of 873 individuals.
These individuals were 54% women, on average 25.6 years old (SDage = 7.2, range = 18-66), 57% were in a relationship, and 40% had a university degree as their highest level of education.
As part of the PEACH study, participants were randomly assigned to the PEACH intervention group (n = 655) or a waitlist control group (n = 218).

Participants selected the following change goals: decrease in Neuroticism (n = 256), increase in Extraversion (n = 196), decrease in Extraversion (n = 1), increase in Conscientiousness (n = 226), decrease in Conscientiousness (n = 24), increase in Agreeableness (n = 35), decrease in Agreeableness (n = 57), increase in Openness (n = 63), and decrease in Openness (n = 15).
Of the 873 individuals who started the study, 531 (61%) also completed the posttest, whereas 342 (39%) did not (Supplemental Figure S1).

text.text: Participants were eligible if they (a) were at least 18 years old, (b) could read German, (c) were not receiving psychotherapeutic or psychiatric treatment, (d) owned a smartphone (Android or iOS) with mobile internet access, and (e) were interested and motivated to participate in an intervention to change a personality trait.
Moreover, participants with mental health disorders and other psychosocial problems were excluded.
Participants were recruited through university mailings, social media advertisements, flyers, and word-of-mouth.
All participants who completed the pretest and follow-up assessment were reimbursed with 25 Swiss Francs.
In addition, they could enter a raffle, where winning chances increased with greater participation.

text.text: During the intervention, participants interacted with the chatbot daily, which delivered the interventional components.

The intervention was grounded in the common change factors model (Allemand & Flückiger, 2017 , 2022), which highlights four key mechanisms for facilitating change: (a) increasing discrepancy awareness between current and desired traits, (b) activating personal strengths and resources and positive expectations, (c) fostering reflective processes to enhance insight, and (d) supporting behavioral practice to master new skills.

text.text: The main goal of the change factor perspective is to optimally realize and integrate all four change factors to maximize intervention effects (Allemand & Flückiger, 2017 , 2022).

text.text: Weekly themes (e.g., building a support network, observational learning, identifying strengths) and microinterventions (e.g., implementation intentions, behavioral activation, self-reflection, individualized feedback) were designed to target these mechanisms.

Microinterventions combined shared techniques, such as reflection on behavioral successes and failures, with trait-specific strategies, for example, practicing extraverted behaviors when targeting Extraversion change (see Stieger et al., 2018 Stieger et al., , 2021 for more details).

text.text: The exact content of the intervention therefore depended on participants' change goals.
We used the EffectLiteR approach (Mayer et al., 2016 (Mayer et al., , 2020) ) to estimate the individual and average treatment effects.
text.formatted: We used the EffectLiteR approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Mayer et al., 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Mayer et al., , 2020) )</ref> to estimate the individual and average treatment effects.

text.text: This approach is based on the specification and estimation of a multi-group structural equation model (MG-SEM) with selected baseline covariates and stochastic group sizes.

Using this model, the expected value on the outcome variable in the intervention condition and the waitlist control condition is estimated for each person according to their values on the baseline covariates.
The difference between these expected values is referred to as the conditional treatment effect (i.e., the treatment effect given a specific pattern of covariate values).
Under certain assumptions, this effect can be interpreted as an individual treatment effect (see Mayer et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Under certain assumptions, this effect can be interpreted as an individual treatment effect (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Mayer et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The average treatment effect in the population, which is usually the focus, corresponds to the unconditional expectation of these conditional effects.

To implement the EffectLiteR approach, we followed several steps (see Supplemental Analytical Strategy for details): First, we specified multi-group measurement models for the outcome variables and the 26 multi-item covariates using full information maximum likelihood estimation.
The different time intervals between measurements in the two groups (1 month in the waitlist control group and 3 months in the intervention group) were adjusted using a linear growth curve model.

Second, based on factor scores and regression models predicting change in the outcome, we selected the covariates in two steps: The number of covariates (k) was determined using repeated 10-fold cross-validation with forward selection, benchmarked against a permutation-based null distribution.

Which covariates filled these k positions was determined via complementary-pairs stability selection (Meinshausen & Bühlmann, 2010; Shah & Samworth, 2013), that is, by re-running the forward selection on random half-samples and retaining the k covariates selected most frequently.
text.formatted: Which covariates filled these k positions was determined via complementary-pairs stability selection <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Meinshausen & Bühlmann, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Shah & Samworth, 2013)</ref>, that is, by re-running the forward selection on random half-samples and retaining the k covariates selected most frequently.

text.text: The selection targeted treatment × covariate interactions (i.e., potential moderators) while always retaining the baseline outcome, treatment, their interaction, and all covariate main effects in the regression models.

Third, we estimated the final MG-SEMs with the selected covariates (Z) and used the intercept g0(Z) and effect g1(Z) functions to test for average treatment effects (null hypothesis: E[g1(Z)] = 0) and their heterogeneity across individuals (null hypothesis: g1(Z) = constant).

Fourth, we calculated and visualized the individual treatment effects and estimated their bivariate relationships with all 34 baseline variables, with standard errors derived from a nonparametric bootstrap.
The selected covariates thus provide the basis on which individual effects are modeled, whereas the subsequent characterization of who benefits draws on all baseline variables.

Fifth, we probed the robustness of these analytic choices in four additional analyses: (a) backward instead of forward selection, (b) a covariate set defined by an error-controlling stability-selection threshold rather than by k, (c) a different assumption about the unobserved change process in the waitlist group (extrapolating the observed 1-month change assuming decelerating rather than linear growth), and (d) excluding potentially careless responders (based on even-odd consistency and longstring for BFI-2 SR and BFI-2-S OR, respectively) and winsorizing outliers (|z| > 3).
text.formatted: Fifth, we probed the robustness of these analytic choices in four additional analyses: (a) backward instead of forward selection, (b) a covariate set defined by an error-controlling stability-selection threshold rather than by k, (c) a different assumption about the unobserved change process in the waitlist group (extrapolating the observed 1-month change assuming decelerating rather than linear growth), and (d) excluding potentially careless responders (based on even-odd consistency and longstring for BFI-2 SR and BFI-2-S OR, respectively) and winsorizing outliers (|z| > 3).

text.text: Finally, in post hoc exploratory analyses, we re-estimated all models separately for each of the nine life domains (modeled as manifest single-item outcomes) and for a unified personality-change outcome (see Supplemental Analytical Strategy).

text.text: First, for gender, the average treatment effect was significant for men (0.249, p = .007) but not for women (0.080, p = .311; difference: -0.17, p = .027).

Under the intervention, both women (0.173) and men (0.184) were expected to improve to a comparable degree, whereas under the control condition the expected change was more favorable for women (0.092) than for men (-0.064).

Second, for observer-reported Openness, the positive association with individual treatment effects reflected both greater expected improvement under the intervention (r = .29, p = .014) and less expected improvement under the control condition (r = -.39, p = .003), with the same pattern for selfreported Intellectual Curiosity (intervention r = .37, p = .015; control r = -.40, p = .033).

Third, for change goal attainability, the negative association arose because higher attainability predicted greater expected improvement under the control condition (r = .25, p = .005) but was unrelated to expected change under the intervention (r = -.06, p = .551).
Note that the three robust correlates were not among the five covariates of the final model.

text.text: In this study, we examined whether a 10-week digital personality change intervention, previously shown to lead to changes in personality traits (Stieger et al., 2021), causally influences life satisfaction, average domain satisfaction, and satisfaction with individual domains on average or for individuals with specific characteristics.
text.formatted: In this study, we examined whether a 10-week digital personality change intervention, previously shown to lead to changes in personality traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Stieger et al., 2021)</ref>, causally influences life satisfaction, average domain satisfaction, and satisfaction with individual domains on average or for individuals with specific characteristics.

text.text: Using the EffectLiteR framework (Mayer et al., 2016 (Mayer et al., , 2020)), we quantified both average and individual treatment effects.
text.formatted: Using the EffectLiteR framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Mayer et al., 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Mayer et al., , 2020))</ref>, we quantified both average and individual treatment effects.

text.text: We then linked interindividual differences in treatment effects to baseline variables, including demographic characteristics, baseline personality traits, baseline well-being, motivational factors, and engagement preferences.
This is consistent with exploring the prescriptive predictive value of baseline variables (Fournier et al., 2009).
text.formatted: This is consistent with exploring the prescriptive predictive value of baseline variables <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Fournier et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: For life satisfaction, we found no evidence for an average effect or for heterogeneity of effects across individuals.

However, for average domain satisfaction, the intervention yielded a positive average effect, concentrated in work-and emotion-related domains, accompanied by meaningful heterogeneity across participants, which was associated with interindividual differences assessed at baseline.
In the following, we discuss these effects in light of previous research and outline implications, limitations, and fruitful avenues for future research.
The treatment effects were d = 0.12 for life satisfaction (not significant) and d = 0.20 for average domain satisfaction.

The stronger treatment effects observed for average domain satisfaction, compared with life satisfaction, suggest that domain-based measures may be closer to the outcomes targeted by the intervention than the global judgment.

Importantly, the two domains with significant average effects (satisfaction with school/work: d = 0.16; satisfaction with daily emotions: d = 0.18) are precisely those most plausibly tied to the change goals chosen by most participants (Increasing Conscientiousness, n = 226, and Decreasing Neuroticism, n = 256; together 55% of the sample).
The effects on satisfaction outcomes were somewhat smaller than the effect on personality traits (d = 0.27), consistent with satisfaction being a more distal outcome.

They were also somewhat smaller than previously reported mean-level changes in satisfaction across the PEACH intervention period (Olaru, van Scheppingen, Stieger, et al., 2023; e.g., life satisfaction: d = 0.28, 0.23, and 0.21 for the change goal of Decreasing Neuroticism, Increasing Extraversion, and Increasing Conscientiousness, respectively).
text.formatted: They were also somewhat smaller than previously reported mean-level changes in satisfaction across the PEACH intervention period <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Olaru, van Scheppingen, Stieger, et al., 2023</ref>; e.g., life satisfaction: d = 0.28, 0.23, and 0.21 for the change goal of Decreasing Neuroticism, Increasing Extraversion, and Increasing Conscientiousness, respectively).

text.text: In contrast to these previous findings, we implemented a clear causal inference strategy by (a) using a novel method to estimate treatment effects (EffectLiteR) rather than pre-post mean-level changes, (b) adjusting for unequal pre-post intervals (3-month intervention vs. 1-month control), and (c) conducting (modified) intention-to-treat analyses, as is best practice for randomized controlled trials.
Further, we included participants with all change goals, yielding a larger and more heterogeneous sample (N = 873 instead of N = 647).
Using this approach, we find evidence that the intervention causally improves domain satisfaction, both on average and for individual domains, with slightly more conservative effect size estimates.

On a broader level, the causal relationships between volitional personality change and domain satisfaction established here carry two key implications: First, given that the traits targeted by the majority of participants (Decreasing Neuroticism, Increasing Extraversion, and Increasing Conscientiousness) are all robustly associated with higher domain-specific satisfaction across multiple life domains (Hudson & Roberts, 2014; Olaru, van Scheppingen, Bleidorn, et al., 2023), our results provide experimental confirmation of these wellestablished cross-sectional associations.
text.formatted: On a broader level, the causal relationships between volitional personality change and domain satisfaction established here carry two key implications: First, given that the traits targeted by the majority of participants (Decreasing Neuroticism, Increasing Extraversion, and Increasing Conscientiousness) are all robustly associated with higher domain-specific satisfaction across multiple life domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Hudson & Roberts, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Olaru, van Scheppingen, Bleidorn, et al., 2023)</ref>, our results provide experimental confirmation of these wellestablished cross-sectional associations.

text.text: This finding is in line with theories that assume causal effects of personality on well-being (e.g., Kroencke et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This finding is in line with theories that assume causal effects of personality on well-being (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Kroencke et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Second, previous research has shown that dissatisfied individuals tend to report stronger change goals (Hudson & Roberts, 2014).
text.formatted: Second, previous research has shown that dissatisfied individuals tend to report stronger change goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Hudson & Roberts, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings suggest that for individuals with such change goals (an inclusion criterion for the intervention), personality change interventions may represent a promising, albeit modest, route to improving well-being.
For life satisfaction, we did not find significant heterogeneity, whereas for average domain satisfaction, and for satisfaction with almost every individual domain, we did.

The presence of heterogeneity is consistent with recent work in clinical psychology, which emphasizes that treatment effects can vary substantially across individuals (e.g., Cohen & DeRubeis, 2018; Kaiser et al., 2022).
text.formatted: The presence of heterogeneity is consistent with recent work in clinical psychology, which emphasizes that treatment effects can vary substantially across individuals (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Cohen & DeRubeis, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Kaiser et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The fact that heterogeneity emerged for domain satisfaction but not life satisfaction reinforces previous arguments that domain-based measures may be more proximal to the intervention outcomes.
The absence of heterogeneity in personality traits may indicate that the intervention changes personality relatively uniformly.
However, it may also reflect methodological limitations (i.e., we combined the traits into a unified outcome variable because we lacked the power to analyze each change goal condition separately).
Disentangling these accounts will require future studies sufficiently powered for trait-specific subgroup analyses (see Strengths, Limitations, and Future Outlook).

On a broader level, our results suggest that the significantly positive effects for average domain satisfaction described above only apply to 27% of participants, while 66% were expected to experience no significant effects and 7% even significantly negative effects.

This finding critically extends recent research highlighting possible negative side effects of personality change interventions (Haehner et al., 2026), such as exhaustion from sustained counterdispositional behavior (Jacques-Hamilton et al., 2019), frustration over unmet goals, or increased self-doubt.
text.formatted: This finding critically extends recent research highlighting possible negative side effects of personality change interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Haehner et al., 2026)</ref>, such as exhaustion from sustained counterdispositional behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Jacques-Hamilton et al., 2019)</ref>, frustration over unmet goals, or increased self-doubt.

text.text: Given the accumulating evidence for intervention outcome heterogeneity, identifying prescriptive variables that indicate who might experience adverse effects is an essential next step to improve effectiveness, prevent potential harmful side effects, and disseminate interventions more responsibly.

Among a broad set of interindividual differences, we identified three prescriptive variables that were robustly associated with stronger well-being increases in the treatment compared to the control condition and that summarize, in terms of directly observable characteristics, the heterogeneity captured by the personality facets in the final model.

As our analysis approach was exploratory, the results should be considered a promising starting point for future confirmatory research, and we can only provide tentative explanations for the observed effects.
First, treatment effects were positive and significant for men, but small and nonsignificant for women.
A closer examination showed that this difference was driven almost entirely by the control condition rather than by differential responses to the intervention itself.

Women, but not men, tended to improve even without the intervention, possibly by seeking psychological support elsewhere, consistent with evidence that men culturally engage in less help-seeking (Addis & Mahalik, 2003).
text.formatted: Women, but not men, tended to improve even without the intervention, possibly by seeking psychological support elsewhere, consistent with evidence that men culturally engage in less help-seeking <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Addis & Mahalik, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Second, participants with higher Openness benefited more from the intervention, consistent with some previous findings from positive psychology interventions (Senf & Liau, 2013).
text.formatted: Second, participants with higher Openness benefited more from the intervention, consistent with some previous findings from positive psychology interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Senf & Liau, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: This association was most robust for observer-reported Openness and pointed in the same direction for the self-reported facet Intellectual Curiosity.
More open individuals improved more under the intervention, possibly because their curiosity and willingness to try new things led them to engage more deeply with the intervention content.
At the same time, they improved less without the intervention, suggesting that their curiosity may require structured input to translate into change.

Third, change goal attainability was positively related to expected improvement under the control condition but unrelated to expected improvement under the intervention, indicating that participants who saw their goal as attainable tended to improve even without the intervention, whereas those who saw it as less attainable depended on it.

For these individuals, the intervention may supply the goal-relevant resources that they otherwise lack in their everyday environments (e.g., situational opportunities to enact the goal, a sense of personal control, and reliable social support).
Regarding baseline well-being, we did not find the negative moderation effect suggested by prior clinical work.

A plausible account is a non-linear (inverted-U) relation: Individuals with intermediate baseline well-being benefit most, whereas those with high baseline well-being show ceiling effects and those with very low baseline well-being require more intensive interventions (e.g., psychotherapy; Gander et al., 2016).
text.formatted: A plausible account is a non-linear (inverted-U) relation: Individuals with intermediate baseline well-being benefit most, whereas those with high baseline well-being show ceiling effects and those with very low baseline well-being require more intensive interventions (e.g., psychotherapy; <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Gander et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, other motivational factors (e.g., implicit theory of personality) and engagement preferences did not robustly predict treatment effects.

This parallels findings from the same intervention that change goal strength, attainability, and beliefs about the changeability of personality did not consistently predict personality change during the intervention (Olaru et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This parallels findings from the same intervention that change goal strength, attainability, and beliefs about the changeability of personality did not consistently predict personality change during the intervention <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Olaru et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, despite observing significant outcome heterogeneity and examining a broad set of interindividual difference variables at baseline, we found few significant associations.
Moreover, although the heterogeneity itself could be demonstrated with high confidence, identifying the covariates responsible for it was subject to larger uncertainty.

This pattern is in line with previous research showing that heterogeneity in treatment effects is difficult to predict (Kaiser et al., 2022; von Hippel & Schuetze, 2025) and points to a need for further work in this area (see Strengths, Limitations, and Future Outlook).
text.formatted: This pattern is in line with previous research showing that heterogeneity in treatment effects is difficult to predict <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kaiser et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">von Hippel & Schuetze, 2025)</ref> and points to a need for further work in this area (see Strengths, Limitations, and Future Outlook).

text.text: In our study, we used a causal inference framework to calculate individual treatment effects of the intervention vs. control group, instead of simply predicting observed pre-post differences in the intervention group.

Our findings illustrate why this matters: Expected improvement under the intervention was nearly identical for women and men and unrelated to change goal attainability, so a prognostic analysis within the intervention group would have missed both associations, which arose from differences in improvement without the intervention.
Thus, the results on prescriptive variables are particularly informative for personalizing intervention choice.

First, our results suggest that personality change interventions offer the greatest added value for men, individuals who are rated higher in Openness by others, and those who perceive their change goal as less attainable.
For women and for individuals with below-average observer-reported Openness, expected treatment effects were essentially null (see Supplemental Table S5).
text.formatted: For women and for individuals with below-average observer-reported Openness, expected treatment effects were essentially null (see Supplemental Table <ref type="table">S5</ref>).

text.text: For women, however, this does not mean that the intervention is ineffective in absolute terms, as they improved under the intervention as much as men did but also improved without it.

Only at very low Openness levels may effects be negative (cf. the 7% of participants with significantly negative individual effects), suggesting that interventions should be administered more cautiously in this group.

Second, researchers could work on developing alternative interventions for individuals who might experience null or even negative effects by either adjusting existing interventions or by suggesting entirely different intervention strategies (e.g., acceptance-or strength-based approaches; Krämer et al., 2025; Peterson & Seligman, 2004).
text.formatted: Second, researchers could work on developing alternative interventions for individuals who might experience null or even negative effects by either adjusting existing interventions or by suggesting entirely different intervention strategies (e.g., acceptance-or strength-based approaches; <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Krämer et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Peterson & Seligman, 2004</ref>).

text.text: As noted above, however, both implications ultimately depend on replicating these exploratory findings in confirmatory research (see also Meinke et al., 2024).
text.formatted: As noted above, however, both implications ultimately depend on replicating these exploratory findings in confirmatory research (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Meinke et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Our study has several strengths.
This work represents the first investigation of heterogeneous treatment effects of personality change interventions on well-being.
Importantly, we examined the prescriptive value of baseline variables, which can specifically inform personalized intervention choice but is rarely examined.
Moreover, we used data from the largest randomized controlled personality intervention to date (Stieger et al., 2018 (Stieger et al., , 2021)), providing an exceptionally high-powered analysis.
text.formatted: Moreover, we used data from the largest randomized controlled personality intervention to date <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Stieger et al., 2018</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Stieger et al., , 2021))</ref>, providing an exceptionally high-powered analysis.

text.text: Our analysis strategy is also consistent with recent methodological recommendations to separate true heterogeneity from estimation noise, benchmark against explicit null distributions, and treat significance claims from many candidate moderators with caution (von Hippel & Schuetze, 2025).
text.formatted: Our analysis strategy is also consistent with recent methodological recommendations to separate true heterogeneity from estimation noise, benchmark against explicit null distributions, and treat significance claims from many candidate moderators with caution <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(von Hippel & Schuetze, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Naturally, however, this work is subject to several limitations, which point to interesting directions for future research.
First, given that this is a secondary data analysis, we encountered several challenges inherent to the original study design.
For instance, the time lag of outcome measurements differed between the intervention group (3 months) and control group (1 month), which we accounted for using a linear growth curve model.
This choice mildly affected the results.
For life satisfaction, for instance, the average effect became significant under the alternative extrapolation.
Future studies should preregister such analytic decisions and the entire data analysis pipeline in advance.
Second, attrition was substantial (39%), as is common in digital interventions.

Because all 873 participants entered the analyses via full information maximum likelihood and dropout was only weakly related to observed baseline traits (Stieger et al., 2021), we consider the risk of bias limited.
text.formatted: Because all 873 participants entered the analyses via full information maximum likelihood and dropout was only weakly related to observed baseline traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Stieger et al., 2021)</ref>, we consider the risk of bias limited.

text.text: However, bias from unobserved determinants of dropout cannot be ruled out, and the effects may generalize primarily to settings with comparable adherence.

Third, while we explicitly opted for an exploratory analysis approach to accommodate our goal of simultaneously evaluating a wide range of potential interindividual difference moderators, our results require confirmation in an independent sample and ideally with a hypothesis-confirming approach.

Given the scarcity of randomized controlled personality intervention studies conducted to date, this will require substantial further research with samples large enough to accommodate moderation analyses.
Because covariates were selected on the same data, the reported p values of correlates (Table 1) are conditional on that selection and thus exploratory.
text.formatted: Because covariates were selected on the same data, the reported p values of correlates (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>) are conditional on that selection and thus exploratory.

text.text: We therefore gauge each association by its consistency across models rather than in isolation.
Fifth, while we examined a broad range of baseline variables spanning sociodemographic, personality, and motivational factors, our selection of variables was naturally limited by the available data.
Other potentially important variables are promising targets for future investigations.
In particular, future work should study the role of ethnicity and culture-related variables to ensure that personality change interventions benefit diverse populations.
Importantly, the estimate of heterogeneity depends on the diversity of the sample and is only accurate if all relevant covariates were included.
Accordingly, studies using larger, more heterogeneous samples and a broader set of baseline variables may uncover even greater interindividual differences.
This study provides the first investigation of interindividual differences in well-being effects of digital personality change interventions.

While the investigated intervention improved average domain satisfaction for a typical individual, particularly in work-and emotion-related domains, we identified remarkable heterogeneity in individual treatment effects on well-being.
Among a broad range of potential correlates, gender, observer-reported Openness, and self-reported change goal attainability were associated with these effects.
These findings underscore that personality change interventions cannot be assumed to work equally well for all individuals.

Future research should investigate more diverse populations, identify further important moderator variables, and, crucially, develop personalization strategies that maximize benefits, minimize harm, and ensure inclusivity.
